title: The Challenge of Achieving Nature‐Positive Net‐Zero Pathways and a Viable Agri‐Food Sector in Australia Without Depleting Catchment Water Resources
content:
Abstract

Australia is committed to achieving net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 2050 and nature-positive targets aligned with the Global Biodiversity Framework and Australia's National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan. Both commitments require changes in land use and management (e.g., reforestation) which could compromise agricultural production and adversely impact water availability. This study assesses the potential of Australia's land sector to simultaneously deliver on its commitments to national net-zero emissions and biodiversity goals, while meeting increasing domestic and export demand for agri-food production, without depleting catchment-scale environmental flows below sustainable limits. Using the Land-Use Trade-Offs model version 2 (LUTO2), we simulated land-use and management pathways across Australia through to 2050 balancing national-scale optimization coverage with fine-scale spatial and temporal detail. Our results show that, under specific modeled scenarios and assumptions of policy support and technology adoption, ambitious GHG emissions and biodiversity targets could be theoretically achieved alongside rising agricultural demand. However, achieving the most ambitious targets in practice would require the conversion of 77.73 Mha of livestock land to non-agricultural uses by 2050, alongside the implementation of agricultural management solutions across 97.49 Mha of cropland. Notably, non-agricultural land uses such as Environmental plantings (mixed native species) emerged as critical for simultaneously delivering biodiversity and GHG emissions targets. These findings define a theoretical feasibility envelope for policymakers, landholders, environmental planners, and industry stakeholders, informing decisions about the type of changes in land-use and management required to support a sustainable, productive, and economically viable transition toward a nature positive net-zero future for Australia.
